summary:
The risks documented for transgender travellers in France concentrate in two settings: detention and the border. In everyday movement, accommodation and services, the country's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition.

Visitors in Nouvelle-Aquitaine stand under the framework of France: rules on identity documents, anti-discrimination law, criminal law and marriage law apply uniformly to this region as to every other, and the national oversight mechanisms documented below operate here without variation. No transgender finding specific to Nouvelle-Aquitaine appears in the sources for this dossier.

Prison placement follows the sex inscribed on identity documents. Article D248 of the French Criminal Procedure Code requires men and women to be held in separate establishments, with the consequence that trans women whose documents are marked male, the great majority of them without sex-reassignment surgery, are placed in men's facilities. A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 records the resulting conditions: one detainee recalled other inmates shouting that they did not want women on the wing, together with threats of violence. Adeline Hazan, controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty, states that transgender detainees, overwhelmingly women, are the group that suffers the most in prison, a finding she illustrates with the case of Kara B., an American trans woman held in what Hazan described as worrying conditions.

The national custodial-inspection authority, the CGLPL, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, following its opinion of 30 June 2010. It records continuing serious violations of the fundamental rights of trans detainees in adult prisons, and none in mental-health establishments, closed educational centres or juvenile detention centres. Its review covered roughly forty transgender detainees, with interviews including eight trans women and one trans man, and inspection visits to the Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station. Saint-Martin-de-Ré, in the Charente-Maritime department, is the one inspected establishment situated within Nouvelle-Aquitaine.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of identity documents in public; an account published in StreetPress on 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of questioning by French border police at an airport, conducted in front of other travellers. The Défenseur des droits has issued a framework decision on trans rights confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony, citing a 2023 survey in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and setting out guidance for service providers. For partner recognition, the baseline is the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013, under which France's first same-sex wedding was performed on 29 May 2013.
tangentialFactors:
Adeline Hazan's assessment that transgender detainees suffer more than any other group in French custody is a national characterisation rather than a regional measurement; the sources do not disaggregate complaints, assaults or placements by region, so the intensity of the problem inside Nouvelle-Aquitaine's prisons cannot be read off the record.

The CGLPL's own review design shows the concentration of findings in adult prisons. Of the four prisons it inspected, one lies in this region and three elsewhere in France, and its finding of no violations in mental-health establishments, closed educational centres and juvenile detention centres provides a contrast setting for visitors assessing where custody risk is actually located.

The 64% identity-discrimination figure the Défenseur des droits draws on is a France-wide survey result from the EU Fundamental Rights Agency; it describes the national environment a visitor enters in Nouvelle-Aquitaine rather than a measurement of this region's accommodation, services or streets.
localsOnly:
Placement in custody is decided by the gender recorded on identity documents, and Article D248 of the French Criminal Procedure Code fixes separate establishments for men and women. Trans women without recognised female documents are held in men's prisons, where accounts describe threats and hostility from other inmates, and where isolation used as a protective measure restricts contact and, in the CGLPL's findings, exposes detainees during strip searches and complicates suicide prevention.

The CGLPL's 25 May 2021 opinion, issued as follow-up to its opinion of 30 June 2010, rests on roughly forty cases, including interviews with eight trans women and one trans man, and on letters received over a decade from detained trans people. It reports no marked improvement since 2010 despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform, and its findings apply to the prisons and police detention facilities across France, including those in Nouvelle-Aquitaine.

Residents seeking redress have the CGLPL as national preventive mechanism and the Défenseur des droits, whose framework decision on trans rights confirms persistent violations and issues guidance for service providers alongside the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 finding that 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination. Legal gender recognition, anti-discrimination protection and marriage recognition, available since the marriage-equality law of 2013, are national entitlements in this region.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory reports a transgender-specific incident, prosecution, detention placement, service refusal or police interaction located within Nouvelle-Aquitaine. The detention and border findings are national in scope; whether any of the Article D248 placements or document checks described have occurred in this region is not sourced here.

Which French airport the StreetPress account of 7 March 2017 concerns is not stated in the inventory, so the border-fragmentation account cannot be assigned to an arrival point in this region.

The CGLPL's inspection visits named four prisons and one central police station; the inventory does not say whether any trans detainee interviewed for the opinion was held in the Charente-Maritime establishment located here, only that the site was visited.

The BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 illustrates prison conditions through individual accounts and an official's statement; the inventory provides no count of trans detainees held in Nouvelle-Aquitaine and no data on outcomes, disciplinary measures or complaints from establishments in this region.
